topic: Law fact / myth-buster: a maintenance order does not pay itself - execution, no fresh plea every month, 6-month deadline for execution in UP (Data Ram v. State of U.P., Allahabad HC, Oct 2026; Mala Kumari v. State of U.P., 2026:AHC:152860)

slides.title: Won maintenance? The money won't **come by itself**
slides.subtitle: Three common myths about getting a maintenance order **enforced**, and what the Allahabad High Court says.
slides.cite: **Data Ram v. State of U.P.**, 2026 LiveLaw (AB) 851 · **Mala Kumari v. State of U.P.**, 2026:AHC:152860 · Justice Praveen Kumar Giri

slides.label: Myth 1
slides.title: "The order **is enough**"
bullets: **Fact:** if payment stops, you have to ask the court to **enforce** the order through an **execution application**.
It is filed under **Section 125(3)** CrPC (now Section 144(3) BNSS) or **Section 128** CrPC.
In an order reported on **16 October 2026**, the High Court told all UP trial courts to decide these within **six months**.
slides.note: **Law fact:** the six-month rule comes from the Supreme Court's 2025 ruling in **Periyammal v. V. Rajamani**. Courts that ignore it may face **contempt**.

slides.label: Myth 2
slides.title: "A new case for every **missed month**"
bullets: **Fact:** a maintenance order creates a **continuing** duty to pay, for as long as it stays in force.
In Mala Kumari (2026), the High Court said a wife does **not** need to file a fresh execution plea for each monthly default.
A family court cannot **close** the execution case just because the husband paid one month's dues.

slides.label: Myth 3
slides.title: "If he won't pay, **nothing** can be done"
bullets: **Fact:** courts can order payment straight into the claimant's verified **bank account**.
If he is salaried, his **employer** can be told to deduct it from his pay. His **property** can be attached.
If that is not enough, the court can order **simple imprisonment** of up to one month for each month's default.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: Delay can **cost you**
bullets: In Data Ram, a husband challenged the order **645 days late**. The court refused to excuse the delay and dismissed his plea.
Whichever side you are on, act **on time** and keep a record of every payment.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

caption:
Got a maintenance order but the money still isn't coming? You are not alone, and the law has answers 💰⚖️

Myth 1: "The order is enough." No. If payments stop, you must file an execution application to enforce it. The Allahabad High Court has now told every trial court in Uttar Pradesh to decide such applications within six months, following the Supreme Court's 2025 ruling in Periyammal. Ignoring this may amount to contempt.

Myth 2: "I need a new case every time he misses a month." No. A maintenance order is a continuing duty. The High Court has held that a wife does not have to file a fresh execution plea for each default, and the case cannot be closed just because one month's dues were paid.

Myth 3: "If he refuses, nothing can be done." No. Courts can send the money straight to the claimant's bank account, ask an employer to deduct it from salary, attach property and, as a last step, order simple imprisonment of up to one month for each month's default.

Cases: Data Ram v. State of U.P., 2026 LiveLaw (AB) 851 | Mala Kumari v. State of U.P., 2026:AHC:152860
Bench: Justice Praveen Kumar Giri, Allahabad High Court
